titulo.texto: Fluted Clovis and Lerma Projectile Points

frase_gancho.texto: A stone edge that changed the way giants were hunted.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave the nomadic hunters behind to reach the first village. Step into the Preclassic Hall, where clay replaces stone and houses, figurines, and festivities appear.

guion_corto.texto: These stone points look small, but they were used to hunt the giants of the Pleistocene. The most famous are the Clovis points, with a groove at the base called a flute, where the wooden shaft was fitted. Folsom points are smaller, with a longer groove; and Lerma points are leaf-shaped. All of them were made by striking and pressing the stone with patience and a great deal of knowledge: each point is the work of several hours, and one mistake at the end can ruin everything. That they are found across the whole continent shows something important: the first Americans shared techniques and traveled enormous distances, from Canada to southern Mexico.

guion_largo.texto:
If you have ever tried to break a stone to get a sharp edge, you know it is not easy. Now imagine doing it to make a point that is symmetrical, thin, and sharp on both faces. That is the skill behind these pieces. The process began with a block of flint, chert, or obsidian. First, large flakes were removed with blows from another stone. Then, with a bone or a deer antler, the edge was pressed to detach thin flakes, one after another, until the point had its final shape. It was work for both hands and mind: one mistake at the end could ruin hours of labor.

The hardest part of a Clovis point is precisely its most distinctive feature: the flute. With a precise blow from the base, a long flake was struck off along the length of the piece, leaving a kind of channel. Many people wonder why. The answer is practical: the channel thinned the base and allowed it to fit snugly into the end of a shaft, bound with sinew and resin. Many points broke with that last blow, so those who succeeded were, without a doubt, highly skilled specialists.

Folsom points, smaller and with a groove that covers almost the entire face, are associated with the hunting of the ancient bison, a more agile animal. And Lerma points, leaf-shaped, come from somewhat later times. Over time, the size of the prey changed, and the point changed too.

These points were set into spears or into darts that were thrown with a spear-thrower, also called an atlatl, a lever that gave the arm much more force. The bow and arrow did not yet exist in these lands; they would arrive thousands of years later. That is why the mindset of the hunt was different: hunters had to get very close, and teamwork was vital.

The names have their own history. Clovis comes from a town in New Mexico, where the first ones appeared in 1932. Folsom comes from another, also in New Mexico, where a cowboy named George McJunkin, who was born enslaved in Texas, noticed some enormous bones in 1908. In time, his discovery proved that humans had hunted extinct bison. A man with no scientific degree changed, without knowing it, the history of American archaeology.

The stone itself also travels with us. Obsidian, that black volcanic glass, was already used in these points, and centuries later it would become the raw material for the blades of Teotihuacán, for Mexica weapons, and even for a monkey-shaped vessel that you will see in the Mexica Hall. The same rock that was used to hunt mammoths ended up turned into jewelry.

And here the story of this hall comes to a close. When the climate warmed and the great animals disappeared, these points stopped being the main tool. The groups learned to live on seeds, to observe how they grew, to store them. Little by little a new way of life was born, with an invention more powerful than any point: planting.

texto.Culture: Pre-agricultural hunter-gatherers of the Lithic Stage
texto.Material: Flint, chert, and obsidian flaked by percussion and pressure
texto.Origin: Northern Mexico, Durango, and the Basin of Mexico (Santa Isabel Iztapan)
texto.Dimensions: Clovis point: 8.2 x 2.0 x 1.0 cm; Lerma points: 4.5 to 7.0 cm long

texto.pregunta: Myth: Clovis points were arrowheads shot with a bow.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were spear or dart points, thrown with a spear-thrower; the bow and arrow would arrive in these lands thousands of years later.
